Homework 02

Question 1: Training and test error under a fixed design

Consider a linear regression problem with \(n=100\) observations and \(p=20\) available covariates. Generate one matrix \(\mathbf X_{\mathrm{all}}\in\mathbb R^{n\times p}\) whose entries are independent \(\mathcal N(0,1)\) random variables, and then keep this realized matrix fixed. Let

\[ \beta_j=0.4^{\sqrt{j}}, \qquad j=1,\ldots,p, \]

and define

\[ \boldsymbol\mu=\mathbf X_{\mathrm{all}}\boldsymbol\beta. \]

Generate one training response and one independent test response from

\[ \begin{aligned} \mathbf y &=\boldsymbol\mu+\boldsymbol\epsilon,\\ \mathbf y^* &=\boldsymbol\mu+\boldsymbol\epsilon^*, \end{aligned} \]

where

\[ \boldsymbol\epsilon,\boldsymbol\epsilon^* \overset{\mathrm{ind}}{\sim} \mathcal N_n(\mathbf 0,\mathbf I_n). \]

Here \(\mathbf I_n\) is the \(n\times n\) identity matrix.

For \(m=0,1,\ldots,p\), fit a linear model with an intercept and the first \(m\) columns of \(\mathbf X_{\mathrm{all}}\) using \(\mathbf y\). If \(\widehat{\mathbf y}_m\) is its fitted mean vector, define

\[ \operatorname{MSE}_{\mathrm{train},m} =\frac{1}{n} \left\lVert \mathbf y-\widehat{\mathbf y}_m \right\rVert_2^2, \]

and

\[ \operatorname{MSE}_{\mathrm{test},m} =\frac{1}{n} \left\lVert \mathbf y^*-\widehat{\mathbf y}_m \right\rVert_2^2. \]

Repeat this process independently 200 times, keeping \(\mathbf X_{\mathrm{all}}\) fixed.

Use seed 43202 before generating \(\mathbf X_{\mathrm{all}}\) and the response errors. R and Python use different random-number generators, so their exact numerical values need not agree.

  1. For each \(m\), calculate the average training and test MSE over the 200 simulation runs. Plot both curves against \(m\). Verify numerically that training MSE does not increase as predictors are added in each simulation run.

  2. For the model containing the first \(m\) predictors, write

\[ \mathbf X_m = [\mathbf 1,\mathbf x_1,\ldots,\mathbf x_m], \qquad \mathbf H_m = \mathbf X_m (\mathbf X_m^{\mathsf T}\mathbf X_m)^{-1} \mathbf X_m^{\mathsf T}. \]

Here \(\mathbf X_m\in\mathbb R^{n\times(m+1)}\) and \(\mathbf H_m\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}\). The model has \(m+1\) fitted coefficients, including the intercept. Define its total squared approximation bias as

\[ B_m^2 =\left\lVert (\mathbf I_n-\mathbf H_m)\boldsymbol\mu \right\rVert_2^2. \]

Thus, \(B_m^2/n\) is the mean squared approximation bias.

Calculate the two theoretical expectations

\[ E\!\left( \operatorname{MSE}_{\mathrm{train},m} \mid \mathbf X_{\mathrm{all}} \right) =\frac{B_m^2}{n}+1-\frac{m+1}{n}, \]

and

\[ E\!\left( \operatorname{MSE}_{\mathrm{test},m} \mid \mathbf X_{\mathrm{all}} \right) =\frac{B_m^2}{n}+1+\frac{m+1}{n}. \]

Add these expectations to your plot and compare them with the simulation averages.

  1. Add the test MSE curve from one simulation run to the plot. Explain why this single curve is less smooth than the average test MSE. Use the approximation-bias and estimation-variance terms in the expected test MSE to explain why training MSE cannot be used by itself to select the predictor count.
Show the starter code 
set.seed(43202)

n <- 100
p <- 20
repetitions <- 200

# Generate X_all only once and keep it fixed.
X_all <- matrix(rnorm(n * p), nrow = n)
beta <- 0.4^sqrt(1:p)
mu <- drop(X_all %*% beta)

# Rows represent simulation runs; columns represent m = 0, ..., p.
train_mse <- matrix(NA_real_, nrow = repetitions, ncol = p + 1)
test_mse <- matrix(NA_real_, nrow = repetitions, ncol = p + 1)

for (k in seq_len(repetitions)) {
  # Generate independent training and test responses for this simulation.
  y_train <- mu + rnorm(n)
  y_test <- mu + rnorm(n)

  for (m in 0:p) {
    X_m <- cbind(1, X_all[, seq_len(m), drop = FALSE])

    # Fit the current model using only the training response.
    fit_m <- lm.fit(x = X_m, y = y_train)
    y_hat <- fit_m$fitted.values
    # Store the training and test MSE for this simulation and model size.
    train_mse[k, m+1] <- mean((y_train - y_hat)^2)
    test_mse[k, m+1] <- mean((y_test - y_hat)^2)
  }
}

# Average the MSE values over all 200 simulation runs for each model size.

average_train_mse <- colMeans(train_mse)
average_test_mse <- colMeans(test_mse)

# Hint: apply diff() to every row of train_mse and allow a small
# numerical tolerance when checking that all differences are nonpositive.
check_run <- apply(train_mse, 1, function(x) all(diff(x) <= 1e-10))
training_is_nonincreasing <- all(check_run)

theory_train <- numeric(p + 1)
theory_test <- numeric(p + 1)

for (m in 0:p) {
  X_m <- cbind(1, X_all[, seq_len(m), drop = FALSE])

  # Project the true mean onto the columns of X_m.
  Q <- qr.Q(qr(X_m))
  projected_mu <- drop(Q %*% crossprod(Q, mu))

  # Calculate the mean squared approximation bias for the current model.
  bias_mse <- mean((mu - projected_mu)^2)
  # Store the theoretical expected training and test MSE values.
  theory_train[m+1] <- bias_mse + 1 - (m + 1) / n
  theory_test[m+1] <- bias_mse + 1 + (m + 1) / n
}

# Combine the simulation averages, theoretical expectations, and one
# individual test-MSE run in a data frame for plotting.
results_r <- data.frame(
  m = 0:p,
  train = colMeans(train_mse),
  theory_train = theory_train,
  test = colMeans(test_mse),
  theory_test = theory_test,
  first_test = test_mse[1, ]
)

matplot(
  results_r$m,
  results_r[, c(
    "train",
    "theory_train",
    "test",
    "theory_test",
    "first_test"
  )],
  type = "l",
  lty = c(1, 2, 1, 2, 3),
  lwd = c(2, 2, 2, 2, 1),
  col = c("blue", "blue", "red", "red", "gray"),
  xlab = "Number of predictors",
  ylab = "Mean squared error"
)

legend(
  "topright",
  legend = c(
    "Average training",
    "Expected training",
    "Average test",
    "Expected test",
    "Test from simulation 1"
  ),
  col = c("blue", "blue", "red", "red", "gray"),
  lty = c(1, 2, 1, 2, 3),
  lwd = c(2, 2, 2, 2, 1),
  bty = "n"
)

The test-MSE curve from one simulation is less smooth because it still contains random variance from one particular training response and test response. Averaging across 200 simulations reduces this random variance, producing a smoother curve.

The expected training MSE contains \(-(m+1)/n\) instead of \(+(m+1)/n\), so the expected training MSE is too optimistic about future prediction. Adding predictors usually reduces approximation bias, but at the same time, it also increases estimation variance there are more coefficients to estimate. Training MSE does not show this trend correctly because it is still evaluating using the same data used to fit it. As predictors are added, the model can fit both the true relationship and some training noise, so training MSE keeps decreasing. Therefore, we can’t use training MSE alone to choose the number of predictors.

Question 2: Prediction error at one target point

Let \(n=100\), \(p=6\), and \(\sigma^2=1\). Construct the fixed covariate matrix \(\mathbf X_{\mathrm{all}}\in\mathbb R^{n\times p}\) with entries

\[ (\mathbf X_{\mathrm{all}})_{ij} =\sqrt{2}\cos\left\{ \frac{\pi j(i-\tfrac12)}{n} \right\}, \qquad i=1,\ldots,n, \quad j=1,\ldots,p. \]

Its columns satisfy

\[ \mathbf 1^{\mathsf T}\mathbf X_{\mathrm{all}}=\mathbf 0^{\mathsf T}, \qquad \frac{1}{n}\mathbf X_{\mathrm{all}}^{\mathsf T}\mathbf X_{\mathrm{all}}=\mathbf I_p. \]

Here \(\mathbf I_p\) is the \(p\times p\) identity matrix.

The following code shows a direct construction of \(\mathbf X_{\mathrm{all}}\).

  • R
  • Python
Show the starter code 
n <- 100
p <- 6
X_all <- outer(
  1:n, 1:p,
  function(i, j) sqrt(2) * cos(pi * j * (i - 0.5) / n)
)
#| eval: false
import numpy as np

n, p = 100, 6
i = np.arange(1, n + 1)[:, None]
j = np.arange(1, p + 1)[None, :]
X_all = np.sqrt(2) * np.cos(np.pi * j * (i - 0.5) / n)

Keep \(\mathbf X_{\mathrm{all}}\) fixed and generate one training response from

\[ \mathbf y =\mathbf X_{\mathrm{all}}\boldsymbol\beta+\boldsymbol\epsilon, \qquad \boldsymbol\beta =(0.5,0.5,0.5,0.5,0.5,0.5)^{\mathsf T}, \]

where

\[ \boldsymbol\epsilon \sim \mathcal N_n(\mathbf 0,\mathbf I_n). \]

Here \(\mathbf I_n\) is the \(n\times n\) identity matrix.

For \(m=0,\ldots,p\), fit a linear model with an intercept and the first \(m\) predictors. Consider prediction of the mean response at

\[ \mathbf x_0=(0,1,0,0,1,0)^{\mathsf T}. \]

Write

\[ \mu_0=\mathbf x_0^{\mathsf T}\boldsymbol\beta, \]

and let \(\widehat\mu_{0,m}\) be the prediction from the model containing the first \(m\) predictors. Here \(x_{0j}\) denotes the \(j\)th coordinate of \(\mathbf x_0\). For this design,

\[ E\!\left[ \left(\widehat\mu_{0,m}-\mu_0\right)^2 \mid \mathbf X_{\mathrm{all}} \right] = \left( \sum_{j=m+1}^{p}x_{0j}\beta_j \right)^2 +\frac{\sigma^2}{n} \left( 1+\sum_{j=1}^{m}x_{0j}^2 \right). \]

  1. Calculate \(\mu_0\), the theoretical squared bias, and the expected squared error for \(m=0,\ldots,p\) using the formula above. You do not need to derive the formula. Briefly explain in words why it consists of a squared bias term from omitted predictors and a variance term from estimating coefficients; no proof is required. Identify the values of \(m\) where the expected squared error changes and where it remains unchanged.

  2. Use seed 43203. Generate the response, fit the models, and calculate

\[ \left(\widehat\mu_{0,m}-\mu_0\right)^2. \]

Repeat this independently 200 times. Plot the simulation averages and theoretical expectations together. Report the smallest \(m\) that minimizes the theoretical error.

  1. All six regression coefficients are nonzero. Explain why only predictors 2 and 5 contribute directly to the mean response at \(\mathbf x_0\). Contrast this target-specific error with the test MSE averaged over all rows of \(\mathbf X_{\mathrm{all}}\) in Question 1.
Show the starter code 
set.seed(43203)

n <- 100
p <- 6
sigma2 <- 1
repetitions <- 200

X_all <- outer(
  1:n, 1:p,
  function(i, j) sqrt(2) * cos(pi * j * (i - 0.5) / n)
)

beta <- rep(0.5, p)
x0 <- c(0, 1, 0, 0, 1, 0)
mu <- drop(X_all %*% beta)

# Calculate the true mean response at the target point x0.
mu0 <- sum(x0*beta)

theory <- data.frame(
  m = 0:p,
  squared_bias = NA_real_,
  variance = NA_real_,
  expected_error = NA_real_
)

for (m in 0:p) {
  # When m = p, there are no omitted predictors.
  omitted_contribution <- if (m < p) {
    # Add the target-point contributions from predictors omitted by the model.
    omitted_indices <- (m+1):p
    sum(x0[omitted_indices] * beta[omitted_indices])
  } else {
    0
  }

  included_x0 <- x0[seq_len(m)]

  # Store squared bias, estimation variance, and the sum for this model.
  theory$squared_bias[m+1] <- omitted_contribution^2
  theory$variance[m+1] <- sigma2/n * (1 + sum(included_x0^2))
  theory$expected_error[m+1] <- theory$squared_bias[m+1] + theory$variance[m+1]
}

print(c(mu0 = mu0))
mu0 
  1

}

minimum_m <- which.min(theory$expected_error) - 1

print(c(minimum_m = minimum_m))

The target mean is \(\mathbf x_0^{\mathsf T}\beta\) = 0.5 + 0.5 = 1 The square-bias term measures the error caused by predictors that are omitted from the model. If the omitted predictor has a nonzero value in \(x0\), the model can’t include the predictor’s contribution to the target mean. The variance term appears because the intercept and included regression coefficients are estimated using a noisy training response. The smallest predictor count minimizing theoretical error is \(m = 5\) Only the second and fifth coordinate of \(x0\) is nonzero, so although all six coefficients are nonzero, since a predictor’s contribution includes \(x0\), the other coefficients are multiplied by zero at this target point. Question 2 measures prediction error at one specific point, whereas Question 1 averages test error over all rows of x_all. Therefore, predictors that do not contribute at \(x0\) may still be important at other points.

Question 3: The optimism correction

Choose one candidate model before observing the response. Let \(p\) be its number of predictors and let \(\mathbf X\in\mathbb R^{n\times(p+1)}\) be its full-rank design matrix, including the intercept. The model has \(p+1\) fitted coefficients. Let

\[ \mathbf H =\mathbf X (\mathbf X^{\mathsf T}\mathbf X)^{-1} \mathbf X^{\mathsf T} \]

be its hat matrix. Suppose

\[ \mathbf y=\boldsymbol\mu+\boldsymbol\epsilon, \qquad \mathbf y^*=\boldsymbol\mu+\boldsymbol\epsilon^*, \]

Conditional on the fixed design \(\mathbf X\), the two error vectors are independent, have mean zero, and have covariance matrix \(\sigma^2\mathbf I_n\). Define

\[ \operatorname{MSE}_{\mathrm{train}} = \frac{1}{n} \left\lVert \mathbf y-\mathbf H\mathbf y \right\rVert_2^2, \qquad \operatorname{MSE}_{\mathrm{test}} = \frac{1}{n} \left\lVert \mathbf y^*-\mathbf H\mathbf y \right\rVert_2^2. \]

The conditional bias vector of the fitted mean is

\[ E(\mathbf H\mathbf y\mid\mathbf X)-\boldsymbol\mu = -(\mathbf I_n-\mathbf H)\boldsymbol\mu. \]

Let \(B^2\) denote the total squared approximation bias:

\[ B^2 =\left\lVert (\mathbf I_n-\mathbf H)\boldsymbol\mu \right\rVert_2^2. \]

Thus, \(B^2/n\) is the mean squared approximation bias.

You may use

\[ \mathbf H^{\mathsf T}=\mathbf H, \qquad \mathbf H^2=\mathbf H, \qquad \operatorname{tr}(\mathbf H)=p+1. \]

For any fixed matrix \(\mathbf A\), you may also use

\[ E\!\left( \boldsymbol\epsilon^{\mathsf T} \mathbf A \boldsymbol\epsilon \mid \mathbf X \right) =\sigma^2\operatorname{tr}(\mathbf A). \]

  1. Derive

\[ E(\operatorname{MSE}_{\mathrm{train}}\mid\mathbf X) =\frac{B^2}{n} +\sigma^2\left(1-\frac{p+1}{n}\right), \]

and

\[ E(\operatorname{MSE}_{\mathrm{test}}\mid\mathbf X) =\frac{B^2}{n} +\sigma^2\left(1+\frac{p+1}{n}\right). \]

  1. Deduce the expected optimism, defined as \(E(\operatorname{MSE}_{\mathrm{test}}-\operatorname{MSE}_{\mathrm{train}}\mid\mathbf X)\). For

\[ n=120, \qquad p=4, \qquad \frac{B^2}{n}=0.04, \qquad \sigma^2=1, \]

calculate the expected training MSE, expected test MSE, and their difference. Explain why the ordering need not hold for every realized pair of responses.

  1. Continue with \(n=120\) and \(p=4\). Suppose the candidate model has residual sum of squares \(\operatorname{RSS}=116.4\), and suppose a common estimate of the error variance is \(\widehat\sigma^2=0.96\).

Calculate

\[ \widehat{\operatorname{MSE}}_{\mathrm{test}} =\frac{ \operatorname{RSS}+2(p+1)\widehat\sigma^2 }{n}, \]

and

\[ C_p =\frac{\operatorname{RSS}}{\widehat\sigma^2} -n+2(p+1). \]

Show how these two quantities are related, and explain why minimizing \(C_p\) is equivalent to minimizing the corrected test MSE when \(n\) and \(\widehat\sigma^2\) are common to all candidate models.

Show the starter code 
# Plug in the values from part (b).
n <- 120
p <- 4
bias_mse <- 0.04
sigma2 <- 1

# The training formula subtracts the complexity term, while test adds it.
expected_train <- bias_mse + sigma2 * (1 - (p + 1) / n)
expected_test <- bias_mse + sigma2 * (1 + (p + 1) / n)

# Optimism is the gap between expected test and training MSE.
expected_optimism <- expected_test - expected_train

print(c(
  expected_train = expected_train,
  expected_test = expected_test,
  expected_optimism = expected_optimism
))
   expected_train     expected_test expected_optimism 
       0.99833333        1.08166667        0.08333333
Show the starter code 
# Now plug in the values from part (c).
RSS <- 116.4
sigma2_hat <- 0.96

# Use p + 1 because the intercept also counts as a fitted coefficient.
corrected_test_mse <- (RSS + 2 * (p + 1) * sigma2_hat) / n
Cp <- RSS / sigma2_hat - n + 2 * (p + 1)

# Check that transforming Cp gives the same corrected test MSE.
test_mse_from_Cp <- sigma2_hat * (Cp + n) / n

print(c(
  corrected_test_mse = corrected_test_mse,
  Cp = Cp,
  test_mse_from_Cp = test_mse_from_Cp
))
corrected_test_mse                 Cp   test_mse_from_Cp 
              1.05              11.25               1.05

For training error, first write the residual as

\[ \mathbf y-\mathbf H\mathbf y =(\mathbf I_n-\mathbf H)\boldsymbol\mu +(\mathbf I_n-\mathbf H)\boldsymbol\epsilon. \]

The cross term averages to zero. Since \(\mathbf I_n-\mathbf H\) is symmetric and idempotent, we get

\[ \begin{aligned} E\!\left(\left\lVert\mathbf y-\mathbf H\mathbf y\right\rVert_2^2\mid\mathbf X\right) &=B^2+\sigma^2\operatorname{tr}(\mathbf I_n-\mathbf H)\\ &=B^2+\sigma^2\{n-(p+1)\}. \end{aligned} \]

After dividing by \(n\),

\[ E(\operatorname{MSE}_{\mathrm{train}}\mid\mathbf X) =\frac{B^2}{n} +\sigma^2\left(1-\frac{p+1}{n}\right). \]

For test error, the residual becomes

\[ \mathbf y^*-\mathbf H\mathbf y =(\mathbf I_n-\mathbf H)\boldsymbol\mu +\boldsymbol\epsilon^*-\mathbf H\boldsymbol\epsilon. \]

The errors are independent, so the cross terms average to zero again. This gives

\[ \begin{aligned} E\!\left(\left\lVert\mathbf y^*-\mathbf H\mathbf y\right\rVert_2^2\mid\mathbf X\right) &=B^2+n\sigma^2+\sigma^2\operatorname{tr}(\mathbf H)\\ &=B^2+\sigma^2\{n+(p+1)\}. \end{aligned} \]

After dividing by \(n\),

\[ E(\operatorname{MSE}_{\mathrm{test}}\mid\mathbf X) =\frac{B^2}{n} +\sigma^2\left(1+\frac{p+1}{n}\right). \]

Subtracting the training result from the test result gives

\[ E(\operatorname{MSE}_{\mathrm{test}}-\operatorname{MSE}_{\mathrm{train}}\mid\mathbf X) =\frac{2(p+1)\sigma^2}{n}. \]

The expected training MSE is \(0.998333\), the expected test MSE is \(1.081667\), and the expected optimism is \(0.083333\). These are long-run averages, so a test MSE can still be smaller than its training MSE in one particular sample.

The corrected test MSE is \(1.05\) and \(C_p\) is \(11.25\). They are related by

\[ \widehat{\operatorname{MSE}}_{\mathrm{test}} =\frac{\widehat\sigma^2(C_p+n)}{n}. \]

When \(n\) and \(\widehat\sigma^2\) are the same for every model, this transformation does not change which model is smallest. Therefore, minimizing \(C_p\) gives the same choice as minimizing the corrected test MSE.

Question 4: Comparing Mallows’ \(C_p\), AIC, and BIC

Use data/diabetes.csv, with y as the response. Use rows 1 through 370 as the training data, and let \(n=370\) denote the training sample size. Do not use rows 371 through 442 in this question. Fit the following ordinary least-squares models, each with an intercept.

Model Predictors \(p\)
Model A bmi, bp, s5, sex, s1, s2, s4 7
Model B all predictors in Model A, followed by s6 8
Full reference all ten predictors 10

Here \(p\) counts predictors, so each model has \(p+1\) fitted coefficients including the intercept. Estimate one common noise variance from the full reference model, using \(p=10\):

\[ \widehat\sigma^2 =\frac{\operatorname{RSS}_{\mathrm{full}}}{n-(p+1)}. \]

For Models A and B, calculate

\[ C_p =\frac{\operatorname{RSS}}{\widehat\sigma^2} -n+2(p+1), \]

\[ \operatorname{AIC}^{\mathrm{red}} =n\log\left(\frac{\operatorname{RSS}}{n}\right)+2(p+1), \]

and

\[ \operatorname{BIC}^{\mathrm{red}} =n\log\left(\frac{\operatorname{RSS}}{n}\right) +(p+1)\log(n). \]

The reduced AIC and BIC omit constants shared by the two candidate models. Smaller values are preferred within each criterion.

  1. Fit the three models. Report \(p\), RSS, the residual degrees of freedom of the full model, and \(\widehat\sigma^2\).

  2. Calculate \(C_p\), reduced AIC, and reduced BIC for Models A and B. State which model each criterion selects. Do not compare numerical values across different criteria.

  3. Compare the improvement in fit from adding s6 with the one-parameter penalty under each criterion. Use this comparison to explain any disagreement. Why does selecting a model not establish that it is the true data-generating model?

Show the starter code 
# Use only the first 370 rows for this question.
diabetes <- read.csv("data/diabetes.csv")
train <- diabetes[1:370, ]
n <- nrow(train)

# Fit Models A and B, along with the full model used to estimate variance.
fit_A <- lm(
  y ~ bmi + bp + s5 + sex + s1 + s2 + s4,
  data = train
)

fit_B <- lm(
  y ~ bmi + bp + s5 + sex + s1 + s2 + s4 + s6,
  data = train
)

fit_full <- lm(
  y ~ age + sex + bmi + bp + s1 + s2 + s3 + s4 + s5 + s6,
  data = train
)

rss_A <- deviance(fit_A)
rss_B <- deviance(fit_B)
rss_full <- deviance(fit_full)
full_residual_df <- df.residual(fit_full)

# Use the full model to get one shared estimate of the noise variance.
sigma2_hat <- rss_full / full_residual_df

# Put the predictor count and RSS for all three models in one table.
model_summary <- data.frame(
  model = c("Model A", "Model B", "Full reference"),
  p = c(7, 8, 10),
  RSS = c(rss_A, rss_B, rss_full)
)

results <- data.frame(
  model = c("Model A", "Model B"),
  p = c(7, 8),
  RSS = c(rss_A, rss_B)
)

# Calculate Cp, reduced AIC, and reduced BIC for Models A and B.
results$Cp <- results$RSS / sigma2_hat - n + 2 * (results$p + 1)
results$reduced_AIC <- n * log(results$RSS / n) + 2 * (results$p + 1)
results$reduced_BIC <- n * log(results$RSS / n) +
  (results$p + 1) * log(n)

# For each criterion, choose the model with the smaller value.
selected_models <- c(
  Cp = results$model[which.min(results$Cp)],
  AIC = results$model[which.min(results$reduced_AIC)],
  BIC = results$model[which.min(results$reduced_BIC)]
)

# Compare the better fit from adding s6 with the extra penalty it causes.
aic_bic_fit_gain <- n * log(rss_A / rss_B)
cp_fit_gain <- (rss_A - rss_B) / sigma2_hat
penalty_comparison <- c(
  aic_bic_fit_gain = aic_bic_fit_gain,
  cp_fit_gain = cp_fit_gain,
  aic_penalty = 2,
  bic_penalty = log(n),
  cp_penalty = 2
)

Model A uses 7 predictors and has an RSS of \(1,098,908.566\). Model B uses 8 predictors and has an RSS of \(1,089,717.057\). The full model uses 10 predictors and has an RSS of \(1,089,451.721\). It has 359 residual degrees of freedom, which gives \(\widehat\sigma^2=3034.684460\).

For Model A, \(C_p=8.116\), reduced AIC is \(2,974.640\), and reduced BIC is \(3,005.948\). For Model B, \(C_p=7.087\), reduced AIC is \(2,973.532\), and reduced BIC is \(3,008.754\).

Based on these values, \(C_p\) and AIC choose Model B, while BIC chooses Model A. Adding s6 improves the AIC and BIC fit term by \(3.108\). This is enough to pass the AIC penalty of \(2\), but not the larger BIC penalty of \(\log(370)=5.914\). For \(C_p\), the improvement is \(3.029\), which is also larger than its penalty of \(2\).

These criteria only tell us which candidate has the better balance of fit and complexity. They do not prove that the selected model is the true model that generated the data.

Question 5: Validation and final test data

Use rows 1 through 370 of diabetes.csv as the training data and rows 371 through 442 as the final test data. Consider eleven nested candidate models. For \(m=0,1,\ldots,10\), the model with \(m\) predictors contains an intercept and the first \(m\) predictors in this order:

age, sex, bmi, bp, s1, s2, s3, s4, s5, s6.

An analyst proposes the following procedure:

  1. Fit all eleven candidate models using the training data.
  2. Calculate the MSE of each model on the final test data.
  3. Select the model with the smallest test MSE.
  4. Report that minimum as the final estimate of prediction error.

The analyst argues that the procedure is valid because the final test data were not used to estimate the regression coefficients.

  1. Identify the first step that misuses the final test data. Explain why the minimum of eleven test MSE values is generally too favorable as an estimate of the selected procedure’s future prediction error.

  2. Rewrite the analysis using five-fold cross-validation within the training data. State how the predictor count is selected, what is refitted, and when the final test data may be used.

  3. Suppose the analyst has already examined all eleven test MSE values. What can still be reported transparently, and what additional data would be needed for a new final evaluation?

Show the starter code 
set.seed(43205)

# Split the data into training rows and final test rows.
diabetes <- read.csv("data/diabetes.csv")
train <- diabetes[1:370, ]
final_test <- diabetes[371:442, ]

predictor_order <- c(
  "age", "sex", "bmi", "bp", "s1",
  "s2", "s3", "s4", "s5", "s6"
)

# Randomly split the training rows into five folds.
fold_id <- sample(rep(1:5, length.out = nrow(train)))
fold_mse <- matrix(NA_real_, nrow = 5, ncol = 11)

# Take turns using one fold for validation and the other four for training.
for (fold in 1:5) {
  fold_train <- train[fold_id != fold, ]
  fold_validation <- train[fold_id == fold, ]

  # Try every model from intercept-only through all ten predictors.
  for (m in 0:10) {
    selected_predictors <- predictor_order[seq_len(m)]

    # reformulate() also handles the intercept-only model when m is 0.
    model_formula <- reformulate(selected_predictors, response = "y")

    # Fit on four folds and check the predictions on the fold left out.
    fold_fit <- lm(model_formula, data = fold_train)
    validation_prediction <- predict(fold_fit, newdata = fold_validation)
    fold_mse[fold, m + 1] <- mean(
      (fold_validation$y - validation_prediction)^2
    )
  }
}

# Average the five validation errors and pick the smallest one.
cv_mse <- colMeans(fold_mse)
selected_m <- which.min(cv_mse) - 1

# Refit the chosen model using all 370 training rows.
selected_formula <- reformulate(
  predictor_order[seq_len(selected_m)],
  response = "y"
)
final_fit <- lm(selected_formula, data = train)

# Finally, use the test data once to check the finished model.
final_prediction <- predict(final_fit, newdata = final_test)
final_test_mse <- mean((final_test$y - final_prediction)^2)

cv_results <- data.frame(
  m = 0:10,
  average_validation_mse = cv_mse
)

print(cv_results, digits = 5)
    m average_validation_mse

8   7                 3198.3
9   8                 3214.4
10  9                 3104.1
11 10                 3132.7
Show the starter code 
print(c(
  selected_m = selected_m,
  final_test_mse = final_test_mse
), digits = 5)
    selected_m final_test_mse 
           9.0         2369.3

The problem starts at Step 2 because the final test responses are being used to compare the eleven models. The smallest test MSE may look especially good partly because of random chance, so reporting that same minimum would make the future error look too low.

A better approach is to leave rows 371 through 442 alone and use five-fold cross-validation on rows 1 through 370. For each predictor count, fit on four folds and calculate MSE on the fold left out. Then choose the predictor count with the smallest average validation MSE, refit it using all 370 training rows, and check it once on the final test rows.

If all eleven test MSE values have already been viewed, they can still be reported as an exploratory comparison. However, they no longer count as an untouched final evaluation. We would need a new independent test set or future observations for a new final check.

Reference

James, Witten, Hastie, Tibshirani, and Taylor, An Introduction to Statistical Learning, Chapters 3, 5, and 6.
